chapter_theme: In the Renunciation sarukkam the teacher closes his account of release, the king resolves to strive for it, his ministers urge him to lay down the crown, and he warns his young sons that both the goddess of wealth and the goddess of the earth are faithless.

cast.role: the unnamed ascetic teacher whose teaching on release the king hears
King Payapati, who resolves on renunciation and warns his sons
the king's ministers, who urge him to give up the crown
the king's young sons, addressed in 2081 to 2089

2069.reading: The teacher says that with the two kinds of deeds gone nothing new can come on this road, and that for the faultless great ascetics there is one broad way, the one leading to the summit, and nothing else to tell.
2069.nuance: The two kinds of deeds (இருவகை வினை) are not named here; they are most likely good and bad deed, but the verse does not say so. சூளிகை in line 3 is read as a summit or pinnacle, a rare word, and line 4 is compressed.

claims.claim: when both kinds of deeds are gone nothing further arises, and release is the one road of the great ascetics

2070.reading: The teacher says that the one born is bound to the objects of his senses, that once those objects have matured he feels desire and hatred, and that by heaping up hidden deeds through them even the dead man meets the same nature again.
2070.nuance: Line 3 says the deeds are gathered where there is no door (வாயிலா); I take this as deeds heaped unseen, which is a reading of a compressed phrase.

claims.claim: desire and hatred toward sense objects pile up deeds that bring the same nature again after death

2071.reading: The teacher says that one who greatly fears this wheel of births resolves on renunciation, becomes pure, guards a conduct full of compassion toward kin and living things, and reaches a greatness free of forgetfulness.
2071.nuance: உறவிக்கண் in line 3 may mean toward kin or toward all that live; the reading keeps both open.

claims.claim: fear of the wheel of births leads to renunciation and a compassionate conduct that ends in a state free of forgetting

2072.reading: The teacher says that when right vision and knowledge shine and the mind has conquered the pride of the senses and is pure, the hero who has long practised the road of meditation reaches the world of release from which there is no return.
2072.nuance: The way is the Jain road of vision, knowledge and conduct, reached by the hero's own effort; nothing in the verse gives a god or a grace any part in it.

claims.claim: release is won by right vision, knowledge, a conquered mind and long meditation, and there is no return from it

2073.reading: The teacher says that the final state belongs to the heroes who have cut desire and craving at the root, and asks whether others can know it.
2073.nuance: கடையிலெண் குணத்தது in line 1 is read as the state of the eight qualities (எண்குணம்) with no end; the sense turns on compressed words and on line 2, which is hard to parse.

claims.claim: the last state of the eight qualities is reached only by those who have cut craving and attachment, and others cannot know it

2074.reading: The teacher says the bliss of release is like the light that pours from a jewel, the coolness of a sandal chip and the scent of a flower close at hand.
2074.nuance: சிவகதி here means the state of release; it does not name Siva. The three pleasant comparisons are all sensory, though the verse is about a state said to lie beyond the senses.

claims.claim: the bliss of the state of release can be shown by comparisons with light, coolness and fragrance

2075.reading: When the faultless ascetic has spoken, the victorious king, who has drunk the nectar of the teacher's word, says he will strive to reach the world where there is no return.
2075.nuance: மாதவ னுரைப்ப is read as the great ascetic speaking; the sage is the one the epic's earlier chapters name as the teacher, but the name does not appear here.
2075.event: Payapati, having drunk the teacher's words, declares that he will strive for release.

claims.claim: a king who has heard the teaching resolves to strive for the final world

2076.reading: The king speaks fittingly that his resolve cannot be hindered and that the world has agreed to it, but the ministers, who have not agreed, answer him.
2076.nuance: The first two lines are hard: போதிகை, விலக்க றக்கதன்று and ஒக்க நன்றுடன்படல் can be read as the king's resolve that none may bar, or as a general maxim of agreement, and who exactly speaks in lines 1 and 2 is not fixed. The verse's last line leads straight into the ministers' words in the next verses.
2076.event: The ministers reply to the king who has announced his resolve.

2077.reading: The ministers ask whether one who lived in a dark pit of unbearable pain, with no comfort from anyone, and who has got out through a door by good fortune, would gladly seek the man who would roll him back in.
2077.nuance: The verse is a simile with the application left unsaid; it is given its sense by 2079, where the ministers urge the king to throw off the crown. உருட்டுவான் ஒருவனை is read as one who rolls him back.

claims.claim: one who has escaped the pit of birth and pain would not choose to go back to it

2078.reading: The ministers add a second image, asking whether one who has fled a heavy prison and escaped would go back into the cruel jail of rough guards.
2078.nuance: Prison and pit are the same figure for worldly life; the ministers' point is made by questions, and the second image repeats the first with a harsher keeper.

claims.claim: one who has escaped the prison of birth would not return to it

2079.reading: The ministers say that one who resolves on the great austerity that ends the disease of birth will not look for ties, and ask the jewel-crowned king to give up the crown.
2079.nuance: Here the king's own counsellors urge the renunciation they might have been expected to oppose; the objection sketched in 2076 resolves into their agreement. The verse's last words ('so the ministers are said to have spoken', என்பவே) pass the speech on as report.
2079.event: The ministers urge Payapati to lay down his crown and renounce.

claims.claim: one resolved on the austerity that ends the disease of birth looks for no ties
a king should give up his crown for release

2080.reading: After the ministers speak, the king rises, calls his young sons with their bright spears, and says this to them without anger.
2080.nuance: இனலிலான் in line 4 is taken as without hurt or anger, the king speaking calmly to those he is about to leave in charge.
2080.event: Payapati calls his sons together to speak to them.

2081.reading: The king tells his sons that the goddess of wealth does not favour the unclear-minded, as the pleasure of the senses is not for the poor, the fruit of dharma for the merciless or the understanding of a text for a restless mind.
2081.nuance: The three comparisons set a lack against what it would need (money for pleasure, compassion for dharma's fruit, steadiness for learning); Lakshmi's favour is put on the same list, so the verse does not say wealth is bad, only that it does not stay with the unwise.

claims.claim: Lakshmi does not stay with those whose minds are not clear

2082.reading: The king bids the wealthy hear the goddess's nature: she leaves the men she has joined and never gives herself to any, wanting always someone new.
2082.nuance: Wealth is a woman who stays with no one; the verse does not say any man can hold her by merit.

claims.claim: the goddess of wealth leaves those she has joined and longs for new men

2083.reading: The king says that when a man's merit is spent the goddess leaves the poor like courtesans who turn their backs on the penniless, and slights everyone, with no friendship for anyone she has reached.
2083.nuance: Line 1 makes wealth depend on merit (புண்ணியம்); the loss is a spent deed, not a changed fortune. The courtesan simile belongs to the epic's own habit of using the courtesan for fickleness, and it looks at her as the narrator's side does.

claims.claim: wealth leaves a man when his merit is used up, as courtesans leave the poor

2084.reading: The king says that if she stays by one man she hides his good qualities and breeds in him hatred, anger and pride, and makes even the learned look at others with scorn.
2084.nuance: Even her staying does harm; the verse says wealth, not her leaving, is what spoils the learned.

claims.claim: wealth that stays with a man hides his virtues and produces anger and pride

2085.reading: The king says that the wealth of young men who trust courtesans with long arrow-like eyes is spent away, and that such is the nature of those who enjoy the lotus-creeper of the goddess.
2085.nuance: The last two lines are compressed and the link between the lotus-creeper and the courtesans is not spelled out; I take it as Lakshmi again, so the courtesan and the goddess are set side by side.

claims.claim: young men who trust courtesans lose their wealth

2086.reading: The king tells his garlanded sons not to trust her, and says that the ones who love those she scorns as strangers are the learned.
2086.nuance: The verse turns the warning into a rule of choice: attach to the learned, who do not leave. காதலாராபவர் is read as 'those who love', though the text is compressed.

claims.claim: the learned love those whom fortune slights, and the sons should not trust her

2087.reading: The king turns to the goddess of the earth and tells the sons that she has no family and no virtue as her rule, and that she goes along with men who are clever in strategy.
2087.nuance: The earth is spoken of as a woman who follows the strong and cunning king; the verse does not say whether the sons should fight for her. உலமிகு வயிரத்தோள் in line 4 is a praising address to the sons.

claims.claim: the earth has no family or virtue she keeps to and follows those skilled in stratagem

2088.reading: The king says that the earth has enjoyed more men than there are grains of sand and left them, and has not stayed even with those who came after, which is her nature even now.
2088.nuance: மூரித் தானையீர் addresses the sons as men with great armies; the verse tells them they are one more in a long line.

claims.claim: the earth has left every king who held her and stays with none

2089.reading: The king says that she has no bond with the victorious crowned kings, clings to no one, and keeps only those who cling to her, like an old woman between her watery clothes.
2089.nuance: The close of the line, முற்றுநீர்த் துகிலிடை முதுபெண் நீர்மையே, is hard: it may be an old woman wrapped in a wet cloth or a figure taken from the sea-girt earth. The reading is held loosely.

claims.claim: the earth has no real tie to any king and clings only to him who clings

links.note: 2070 traces how birth turns to desire and hatred toward sense objects, heaps up deeds and brings the same nature back after death; Kural 349 says that the very moment attachment ends, births are cut.
links.teaches: The couplet's moment of cutting is shown in 2070 to be the point where the chain from senses to desire to deed to return is broken.

gains.a: The chain of sense, craving, deed and rebirth gets a plain statement of where it ends, which 2070 leaves unsaid.
gains.b: The couplet gets the working of the births it cuts: attachment makes deeds, and the deeds are what bring the return.

links.note: 2072 has the hero reach release by his own vision, knowledge, mastered mind and long meditation; Tirumanthiram 126 has the freed ones climb the thirty-six tattvas as a ladder to release, enter the light of bliss and see Sivam.
links.teaches: Both texts describe release as a climb by stages, but 2072 ends in a world of release won by the self's own effort while Tirumular's ladder ends in seeing Sivam.

gains.a: The hero's path gets a counter-picture in which the top of the ladder is a seen god, which the verse, with no god in it, does not have.
gains.b: The ladder gets a way of release in which the climber is complete without the vision of a lord, which the couplet does not allow.

links.note: 2074 uses three pleasant senses, jewel-light, sandal coolness and flower scent, for the bliss of release, which it calls சிவகதி; Tirumanthiram 325 uses a drink, the nectar of Siva's bliss in samadhi, for the same kind of state.
links.teaches: Both reach for sensory pictures of a state they say is beyond the senses, but the Jain verse's சிவகதி names a state of release while Tirumular's Siva is the god whose bliss it is.

gains.a: The comparison to light, cool and scent gets a drink image that shows the bliss as unbroken from sitting to lying, which 2074 does not say.
gains.b: The drink of bliss gets a calmer set of images that carry no hint of the intoxication Tirumular is guarding against in this chapter.

links.note: 2075 has the king resolve, after hearing the teacher, to strive for the final world; verse 355 has the counsellor repeat the sage's word that the hero will not be dazzled by kings' wealth and will reach the state of release by austerity.
links.teaches: The sage's early prediction that the king will refuse kings' wealth is kept in 2075, where the king himself declares the resolve.

links.note: 2018 names the lamp of vision as seeing the true thing and says that, once lit, the darkness of deeds cannot stay; 2072 shows the path in which vision and knowledge, with meditation, lead on to the world of release.
links.teaches: The lamp of vision in 2018 is a first step; 2072 sets out what must follow it before the deeds are gone and release is reached.

links.note: 2079 has the king's own ministers urge him to give up the crown for the austerity that ends the disease of birth; Naladiyar 53 says the best people, seeing that home, youth, wealth and strength do not last, renounce them without delay.
links.teaches: Naladiyar 53 describes a person giving up a house and wealth, but 2079 shows the same renunciation asked of a king, where the crown and a kingdom's charge must be laid down.

gains.a: The ministers' plea gets a general rule, that the wise renounce on seeing that things do not last, to rest on.
gains.b: The quatrain gets a case in which what is given up is a kingdom and its cost to others, which a householder's renunciation does not show.

links.note: 2082 makes wealth a woman who leaves the men she has joined and always wants someone new; Kural 332 says great wealth comes like a crowd gathering at a dance hall and goes like the crowd breaking up.
links.teaches: The couplet's crowd goes without any reason in itself; in 2082 the going has a will, the goddess who tires of her man and wants another.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets an image of a crowd that comes and goes for its own reasons and owes the owner nothing.
gains.b: The crowd gets a person with a wish behind its going, so wealth's departure reads as desertion and not only as an end.

links.note: 2083 compares the departing goddess of wealth to courtesans who leave the penniless; Naladiyar 371 says harlots' friendship ends when the hand is empty, as a lamp's light ends when the oil is gone.
links.teaches: The epic turns the Naladiyar's warning about courtesans into a figure for wealth itself, so a man is asked to see in his fortune the same cold arithmetic.

gains.a: The goddess's leaving gets a plain reason, that the love was only for what the hand held, which 2083 leaves implied.
gains.b: The warning about courtesans gets a larger target: the same trade-friendship is shown to run through wealth and fortune, not only through women.

links.note: 2086 tells the sons not to trust the goddess and to love the learned, whom she scorns; Tirumanthiram 169 calls bewildering wealth a waning moon and bids the reader seek the king of the gods, who becomes great wealth like a rain cloud.
links.teaches: Both give up trusting wealth but name different things to trust in its place: the Jain king names the learned, Tirumular names a god who is himself wealth.

gains.a: The advice to attach to the learned gets a rival answer, a lord who stays, so a reader sees that the choice of refuge is itself a doctrine.
gains.b: The rain-cloud wealth of the Lord gets a worldly alternative in which the refuge is people, not a god, and it is held without worship.

links.note: 2088 says the earth has enjoyed countless men and left them, and has not stayed with the next; Siddhar 286 says crowned kings are burnt to a fistful of ash and become earth.
links.teaches: The two reverse the same image: the king thinks he holds the earth, but 2088 says she leaves him and the Siddhar says he is returned into her.

gains.a: The earth that deserts kings gets an ending, that the kings she leaves are laid in her as ash, which the verse does not state.
gains.b: The Siddhar's ash gets a living figure for earth, the woman who goes from king to king, so the fact of burning is given a reason.

source_issues: Verse 2072 line 1 carries a repair of a pulli after a vowel sign; no sense is affected.
Verses 2069, 2070, 2073, 2076, 2077, 2085 and 2089 have compressed or doubtful lines; they are marked uncertain.
The teacher is named by no word in 2069 to 2074 and is taken from 2075 line 1 as the speaker.
